question:
A 35-year-old man, with a history of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) diagnosed 2 years ago, presents with hearing loss in the right ear and tinnitus. Patient says that symptoms have been gradually progressive. He has difficulty hearing speech as well as loud sounds. He also gives a history of occasional headaches and vertigo on and off for 1 month, which is unresponsive to paracetamol. His vitals include: blood pressure 110/78 mm Hg, temperature 36.5°C (97.8°F), pulse 78/min and respiratory rate 11/min. Tuning fork tests reveal the following:
  Left Right
Rinne’s test  Air conduction > bone conduction  Air conduction > bone conduction
Weber test Lateralized to left ear 
Other physical examination findings are within normal limits. An MRI of the head is ordered which is as shown in image 1. A biopsy is done which shows cells staining positive for S100 but negative for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). The histopathological slide is shown in image 2. What is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) -> bilateral vestibular schwannomas -> hearing loss and tinnitus -> progressive symptoms -> difficulty hearing speech and loud sounds -> occasional headaches and vertigo -> unresponsive to paracetamol -> normal vital signs -> normal physical examination findings -> MRI head showing bilateral vestibular schwannomas -> biopsy positive for S100, negative for GFAP -> Most likely diagnosis: Schwannoma -> opc. Schwannoma -> 95%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 35-year-old man with NF2 presenting with hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, and vertigo is Schwannoma, supported by the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas on MRI and positive staining for S100 on biopsy. The patient's symptoms and findings are consistent with this diagnosis.
analysis: The core medical principle guiding this case is the association of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) with bilateral vestibular schwannomas. The patient's symptoms of hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, and vertigo, along with the MRI findings of bilateral vestibular schwannomas and positive staining for S100 on biopsy, strongly support the diagnosis of Schwannoma in this context.
